content: The human nose is the prominent structure on the face that contains the nostrils. Its shape is primarily determined by the ethmoid bone and the nasal septum, which is largely composed of cartilage and serves to separate the nostrils. Due to the unique vascular anatomy of the nose and its surrounding regions, infections originating in the nasal area can potentially spread retrogradely to the brain. This anatomical region, encompassing the area from the corners of the mouth to the bridge of the nose (including the nose and maxilla), is referred to by medical professionals as the danger triangle of the face. The human nose exhibits a wide variety of shapes. Historical attempts have been made to classify these shapes, such as in the 19th-century work Nasology by Eden Warwick (a pseudonym for George Jabet). This text humorously linked nose shapes to personality traits, parodying the pseudoscience of phrenology. The classifications include: Class I: The Roman or Aquiline Nose – Characterized by a convex, undulating shape resembling an eagle's beak. Class II: The Greek or Straight Nose – Defined by a perfectly straight profile. Class III: The Nubian or Wide-Nostrilled Nose – Broad and thick, with a gradual widening from below the bridge, often viewed from the front rather than the side. Class IV: The Hawk Nose – Highly convex, resembling a bow, and thin with a sharp appearance. Class V: The Snub Nose – A short and slightly upturned nose. Class VI: The Turn-Up or Celestial Nose – Features a continuous concavity from the eyes to the tip. In Western cultures, some individuals undergo rhinoplasty to alter the aesthetic appearance of their nose. Nose piercings, such as those on the nostrils, septum, or bridge, are also common. In New Zealand, the Maori people traditionally greet one another with a nose press, known as hongi, though this practice is now largely reserved for ceremonial occasions. Numerous individuals are famously associated with their noses, either due to their distinctive shape, size, or cultural significance. Examples include: Barbara Streisand – Known for her prominent nose. John Barrymore – Nicknamed The Great Profile. Cyrano de Bergerac – A historical figure and literary character renowned for his large nose. Adrien Brody – Recognized for his distinctive nose. Tom Cruise – Declined rhinoplasty early in his career. Jimmy Durante – Frequently referenced for his large nose, humorously depicted by cartoonist Al Hirschfeld. Nanette Fabray – Noted for her small nose. Jamie Farr – Played Klinger on MASH, with many jokes about his nose written into the show. Jennifer Grey – Known for her nose before and after rhinoplasty. W.C. Fields – Recognized for his bulbous nose. Pinocchio – A fictional character whose nose grows when he lies. Bob Hope – Nicknamed ski-nose. Michael Jackson – Underwent multiple nasal surgeries. Major Kovalyov – A character in Nikolai Gogol's The Nose. Barry Manilow – Often parodied for his large nose. Al Molinaro – Known for his role as Al in Happy Days. Jack Nicholson – Featured in Chinatown (1974), where his nose plays a role in the plot. Richard Nixon – Recognized for his distinctive nose. Danny Thomas – Known for his prominent nose. Duke of Wellington – Nicknamed Nosey by his troops due to his large hooked nose. Owen Wilson – Recognized for his unique nasal structure. Tycho Brahe – Lost his nose in a duel and wore a prosthetic made of gold and silver. Severus Snape – A fictional character in J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter series, known for his hooked nose. Gonzo – A Muppet character with a distinctive curved nose. Hector Sepúlveda – Known for his nose in Colegio De San José.
